title: Critical Thinking · Episode 2
chapters: Philosophical razors: shaving away bad explanations
Confirmation bias: the puzzle almost everyone gets wrong

units.t: Critical Thinking. Episode two.
In this episode: Logical fallacies, Philosophical razors: shaving away bad explanations, Confirmation bias: the puzzle almost everyone gets wrong and Probability for everyday life.
Part one. Logical fallacies.
The tricks that make weak arguments sound strong.
You'll hear at least three of these in the next news bulletin.
Arguments with a flaw.
A logical fallacy is a flaw in reasoning that makes an argument seem more convincing than it is.
Fallacies appear in politics, advertising, social media and family dinners.
Sometimes they're deliberate manipulation; often they're honest mistakes.
Naming them helps you think clearly, argue fairly and resist manipulation.
An ad hominem attacks the person instead of the argument: 'Why listen to her views on the economy?
She's never run a business.'
Whether she has run one doesn't decide if she's right.
A related trick is whataboutism, answering criticism by pointing to someone else's faults, which dodges the actual issue.
Straw men and false choices.
A straw man misrepresents someone's position as weaker or more extreme, then knocks that version down.
Someone says, 'We should reduce sugar in school canteens,' and the reply is, 'So you want to ban birthday cake?'
The fairer opposite is the steel man: restating the other side's argument in its strongest form before responding.
A false dilemma presents only two options when more exist.
'You're either with us or against us.'
'Either we build this road or the town dies.'
Real life usually offers a range of options and trade-offs.
When someone gives you just two choices, especially when one is obviously bad, ask what has been left out.
Slopes, crowds and experts.
A slippery slope claims one small step will inevitably end in disaster, without showing why each step follows.
'If students use phones for research, soon they'll be on TikTok all lesson.'
Some chains are real, but each link needs evidence.
The bandwagon fallacy says something is true or good because many people believe it: 'Millions use this remedy.'
Popularity isn't evidence, and plenty of widely held beliefs have been wrong.
An appeal to authority is reasonable only when the person is a genuine expert in the relevant field and reflects expert consensus.
A famous actor's opinion on vaccines, or a single doctor contradicting thousands of others, isn't strong evidence.
Going in circles.
Circular reasoning assumes what it's trying to prove: 'This news site is trustworthy because it says it only reports the truth.'
The conclusion is hidden inside the premise.
A hasty generalisation draws a broad conclusion from too little evidence: 'I got a rude driver twice, so all rideshare drivers are rude.'
Both are easy to fall into when we already believe the conclusion, which is exactly when we should check our own reasoning most carefully.
Use them wisely.
Pointing out a fallacy doesn't prove the conclusion is false.
It only shows that this particular argument for it is weak.
Someone can argue badly for something true.
Assuming a claim is false because it was argued badly is itself an error, sometimes called the fallacy fallacy.
And shouting 'Straw man' in an argument rarely changes minds.
The real value of knowing fallacies is checking your own reasoning and asking better questions of others.
The key idea: A logical fallacy is a reasoning flaw that makes an argument seem stronger than it is, and ad hominem attacks the person instead of the argument.
Part two. Philosophical razors: shaving away bad explanations.
Your car won't start.
Is it a flat battery, or sabotage by a jealous neighbour?
A handful of simple rules called 'razors' can save you from chasing the wrong answer.
What a razor is.
Picture a detective with ten suspects and one afternoon.
She needs a way to decide where to look first.
Thinkers have long used short rules for exactly this job, nicknamed 'razors' because they shave away explanations that are possible but improbable.
A razor never proves anything.
It doesn't tell you the answer is definitely the simple one.
It tells you where the smart money is, so you can spend your attention sensibly.
Think of razors as tie breakers and starting points, not verdicts.
Used well, they stop you getting lost in elaborate theories.
Used badly, as a way to end every conversation, they become a lazy excuse not to think.
Occam's razor.
The most famous razor is named after William of Ockham, an English friar and philosopher who lived around 1287 to 1347.
The slogan 'entities should not be multiplied beyond necessity' was written by later scholars, but the idea runs through his work.
In plain terms: when two explanations fit the facts equally well, favour the one that asks you to assume less.
If your biscuits vanish, a hungry teenager requires one assumption.
A burglar who ignored your laptop and took only the Tim Tams requires several.
Notice the key phrase: equally well.
Occam's razor doesn't say simple explanations are always true.
Complexity has to earn its place by explaining something the simpler version can't.
Hanlon's razor.
A colleague leaves you off an important email chain.
You might think they are freezing you out.
Hanlon's razor suggests a gentler first guess: they probably forgot.

The usual wording is 'never attribute to malice that which is adequately explained by stupidity', credited to a man named Robert Hanlon, who submitted it to a joke book about Murphy's Law around 1980.
A kinder version: don't assume bad intent when busyness, ignorance or a simple mistake would do.
It helps because our brains are quick to see enemies, and it saves friendships and wasted anger.
It isn't naive, though.
If the 'mistakes' keep happening in one direction, the pattern itself becomes evidence.
Hitchens's razor and horses.
Someone says a celebrity is secretly a lizard.
You ask for evidence, and they reply, 'Prove they're not.'
Christopher Hitchens's answer: 'What can be asserted without evidence can also be dismissed without evidence.'
The person making a claim should supply reasons.
You can set it aside until they do.
That doesn't mean it is false.
Medical students learn: when you hear hoofbeats, think of horses, not zebras.
A headache and runny nose is most likely a cold, not an exotic disease.
If your internet drops, a tired router is a horse and a targeted hack is a zebra.
This is about base rates, how often each explanation occurs.
Zebras do exist, so rule out the horses first.
When razors cut wrong.
By the 1840s, astronomers knew Uranus wasn't moving quite as the maths predicted.
The simple response would have been small measurement errors.
Instead, some argued for a more complicated answer: an unseen planet tugging on it.
In 1846, Neptune was found close to where the calculations said it would be.
The elaborate explanation was right because it explained what the simpler one couldn't.
That is how to treat every razor.
People are sometimes genuinely malicious, and zebras sometimes turn up.
When something surprising happens, ask what simple explanation fits all the facts, could it be a mistake, and who is making the claim.
Treat your first answer as a working hypothesis.
A razor that stops you looking becomes a blindfold.
The key idea: A razor is a rule of thumb that shaves away unlikely explanations to show where to look first, without proving anything.
Part three. Confirmation bias: the puzzle almost everyone gets wrong.
Three numbers, one hidden rule, and a mistake that reveals how we all hunt for proof we're right rather than for the truth.
The 2-4-6 puzzle.
In 1960 the British psychologist Peter Wason, at University College London, gave volunteers three numbers: 2, 4, 6.
The sequence followed a rule he had in mind, and their job was to discover it.
They could propose their own sets of three numbers, and he would say whether each fitted.
Most people quickly formed a theory, such as ‘even numbers going up by two’, and tested it with sets like 8, 10, 12.
Every one earned a yes, so they announced their rule, and many were told they were wrong.
The real rule was simply ‘any three numbers in increasing order’.
Tests like 8, 10, 12 fit both the theory and the real rule, so they could never reveal the mistake.
Those who succeeded tried sequences their theory said should fail, such as 1, 2, 3.
Four cards on a table.
Wason's most famous puzzle followed in 1966.
Four cards each have a letter on one side and a number on the other.
You can see E, K, 4 and 7.
The rule is: ‘If a card has a vowel on one side, it has an even number on the other.’
Which cards must you turn over to check whether the rule is being broken?
Most people pick E, and often 4 as well.
E is right.
But 4 tells you nothing, because the rule says nothing about what must be behind an even number.
The card you need is 7: if a vowel is hiding behind it, the rule is broken.
In many studies, only around one person in ten chooses correctly.
Easy when it's about cheating.
Here's the strange part.
Researchers later rewrote the puzzle in familiar terms.
Imagine you are checking a bar where the rule is: ‘If someone is drinking beer, they must be over 18.’
The four cards show: drinking beer, drinking cola, age 25 and age 16.
Which do you check?
Most people quickly pick the beer drinker and the 16-year-old, which is logically the same answer as E and 7.
Studies by Richard Griggs and James Cox in 1982 found that versions like this are solved far more often than the abstract one.
Psychologists still debate why.
Some argue our minds are tuned to spot social cheating; others say familiar situations simply make it obvious which cases could break the rule.
Confirmation bias everywhere.
Wason's puzzles became classic demonstrations of confirmation bias: the tendency to search for, interpret and remember information in ways that support what we already think.
It shows up far beyond the laboratory.
A detective who settles on a suspect early may give extra weight to clues that point their way.
Someone convinced a colleague dislikes them reads every short email as proof.
Investors can seek out news that flatters the shares they already own.
Online, search engines and feeds make it easy to find something that agrees with almost any belief.
The bias isn't stupidity.
Holding on to a working theory saves effort, and often the theory is right.
The danger is that we rarely notice when it isn't.
Try to break your idea.
The lesson from Wason is practical.
When you have a theory, ask: what would I expect to see if I were wrong, and have I looked for it?
Scientists build this into their method by designing experiments that could fail.
You can do a small version in daily life.
Before a big purchase, read the worst reviews, not just the best.
Before deciding someone is untrustworthy, list the evidence that points the other way.

In a 1984 study, Charles Lord and colleagues found that asking people to deliberately consider the opposite reduced biased judgements more effectively than simply telling them to be fair and unbiased.
Testing your ideas like this feels uncomfortable, but it's the quickest route to the truth.
The key idea: Most people test a rule only with examples that fit their theory, so they never see it fail.
Part four. Probability for everyday life.
Why the pokies always win, why a streak of heads means nothing, and how to think clearly about risk.
Chance has no memory.
Probability measures how likely something is, from 0, impossible, to 1, certain.
A 50 per cent chance is 0.
5; a 1 in 4 chance is 0.
A 70 per cent chance of rain means that on days with similar conditions, it rained about 70 per cent of the time.
A fair coin lands heads five times in a row.
What are the odds of heads next?
Still 50 per cent.
The coin has no memory.
Believing tails is now 'due' is the gambler's fallacy.
In 1913 at the Monte Carlo casino, a roulette ball landed on black 26 times in a row, and gamblers lost millions betting that red must come next.
The same applies to lotto numbers, poker machine spins and the sex of a family's next baby.
The house always wins.
Expected value is the average result if you repeated something many times.
If a game costs $1 and gives a 1 in 10 chance of winning $5, you'd spend $10 to win $5 about once: an expected loss of 50 cents a play.
Casino games, poker machines and lotteries are designed this way.
NSW poker machines must return at least 85 per cent of money wagered over time, so players lose up to about 15 per cent of what they wager on average.
The odds of winning division one in Australia's Powerball are about 1 in 134 million.
Buying one game a week, you'd expect to wait around 2.
6 million years.
A ticket is entertainment, not a financial plan.
Coincidences are common.
How many people need to be in a room for a better-than-even chance that two share a birthday?
Just 23.
With 70 people, it's over 99 per cent.
The birthday paradox surprises us because we think about our own birthday matching someone's, rather than any pair matching.
With so many possible pairs, coincidences become likely.
In a country of 27 million people, a 'one in a million' event happens to around 27 people.
Unlikely things happen all the time.
They just don't happen to any particular person often.
Conditional probability.
Probabilities change with information.
The chance that a randomly chosen person is over 190 centimetres is small.
The chance that a professional basketball player is over 190 centimetres is huge.
This is conditional probability, and confusing its direction causes serious errors.
In 1999, English solicitor Sally Clark was convicted of murdering her two baby sons, helped by an expert's claim that two cot deaths in one family had a 1 in 73 million chance.
That figure was flawed.
It also answered the wrong question, because double murder is itself extremely rare.
Her conviction was overturned in 2003.
Thinking about risk.
Our sense of risk is shaped by emotion and familiarity more than numbers.
Risks we choose and control, like driving, feel smaller than imposed ones, like a new phone tower or a food additive, even when the numbers say otherwise.
In Australia you're vastly more likely to die in a car crash than from a shark or snake.
Ask for actual numbers: out of how many people, over what time, compared with what?
Think in probabilities, not certainties: 'maybe a 70 per cent chance this works' encourages you to plan for the other 30 per cent.
Weigh likelihood and impact.
Insure against unlikely but catastrophic losses like a house fire, not minor ones like a scratched phone.
The key idea: Independent events have no memory, so a streak never makes the opposite result 'due'.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. Why is 'She's never run a business, so ignore her economic views' a fallacy?
Answer. It targets the person, not the argument.
Question two. What is a philosophical razor best used for?
Answer. Deciding which explanation to investigate first.
Question three. Why did testing a set like 8, 10, 12 fail to help people in the 2-4-6 task?
Answer. It fitted both their theory and the true rule.
Question four. A fair coin has landed heads five times in a row. What is the chance of heads next?
Answer. Still 50 per cent.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
